scenario.title: Why This Boat?
scenario.premise: Two jobs at one boatyard. Build for what the boat must actually do. This fictional craft story explores Aristotle’s explanations of artifacts, not a claim that nature plans like a boatbuilder.

stage.title: Room for the cart
stage.speaker: The boatbuilder
stage.motivation: The miller needs the loaded cart across the creek. Do not start with just any boat: find how much room its wheels need, then build and use a ferry for that load.
stage.travelText: We are at the yard beside the creek.

objectives.text: Get the loaded cart across the creek.

things.label: Timber stack
things.description: Seasoned planks from the yard. Enough for two small boats; the same wood can be arranged in different ways. This stock is not consumed by one build.

things.label: Measuring cord
things.description: Lay it against what the boat must carry or fit through. The builder sketches the measured outline; the cord does not cut wood.

things.label: Adze
things.description: The boatbuilder uses this to shape and finish an assembled frame. A drawing cannot do this work.

things.label: Pitch pot
things.description: A supply of seam-sealing pitch. It keeps water out; it does not decide what a boat is for.

things.label: Brush
things.description: For working pitch into seams.

things.label: Pole rack
things.description: A supply of long poles to fit out boats for these calm, shallow waters. No wind or sail is needed.

things.label: Loaded cart
things.description: The miller must take this wide, heavy cart across the quiet creek without unloading it. Measure its wheel span before choosing the boat’s shape.

locations.label: Creek landing
locations.description: A broad, calm crossing. A boat must be here to take the cart aboard; simply parking it here does not move the cart.

trace.message: Broad layout. The builder measures the wheels and sketches a broad floor. The intended crossing guides the design; it does not magically reshape timber.

stage.title: The ferry will not fit
stage.speaker: The boatbuilder
stage.motivation: A fisher is stranded beyond the reeds. Our ferry is sound, but too broad for that gap. Measure this new route, then use the same stock and tools to make a boat that can reach the fisher.
stage.travelText: We bring the stock, measuring cord, adze, pitch brush and pole rack for the new job. The working ferry stays at the creek landing.

objectives.text: Bring the stranded fisher safely back through the reeds.

things.label: Sealed skiff hull
things.description: A narrow watertight hull, awaiting propulsion.

locations.label: Reed mouth
locations.description: A fisher waits beyond this shallow gap: narrower than the ferry but wide enough for a two-person skiff. Measure it before building. Bring a suitable boat here to play its outward and return trip.

trace.message: Pole skiff. The skiff is fitted with poles to move through the shallow passage.

scenario.title: Why This Boat?
scenario.premise: Two jobs at one boatyard. Build for what the boat must actually do. This fictional craft story explores Aristotle’s explanations of artifacts, not a claim that nature plans like a boatbuilder.

stage.title: The ferry will not fit
stage.speaker: The boatbuilder
stage.motivation: A fisher is stranded beyond the reeds. Our ferry is sound, but too broad for that gap. Measure this new route, then use the same stock and tools to make a boat that can reach the fisher.
stage.travelText: We bring the stock, measuring cord, adze, pitch brush and pole rack for the new job. The working ferry stays at the creek landing.

objectives.text: Bring the stranded fisher safely back through the reeds.

things.label: Timber stack
things.description: Seasoned planks from the yard. Enough for two small boats; the same wood can be arranged in different ways. This stock is not consumed by one build.

things.label: Measuring cord
things.description: Lay it against what the boat must carry or fit through. The builder sketches the measured outline; the cord does not cut wood.

things.label: Adze
things.description: The boatbuilder uses this to shape and finish an assembled frame. A drawing cannot do this work.

things.label: Pole rack
things.description: A supply of long poles to fit out boats for these calm, shallow waters. No wind or sail is needed.

things.label: Pitch brush
things.description: A reusable brush and supply of pitch for sealing the shaped hulls.

things.label: Slim layout
things.description: The measured passage sets a narrow outline, with room for rescuer and fisher. Reaching that person, rather than carrying the cart, now organizes the work.

things.label: Pole skiff
things.description: Fits the measured reed passage and carries rescuer and fisher. Too narrow for the cart. Bring it to the reed mouth to make the rescue trip.

locations.label: Reed mouth
locations.description: A fisher waits beyond this shallow gap: narrower than the ferry but wide enough for a two-person skiff. Measure it before building. Bring a suitable boat here to play its outward and return trip.

trace.message: Fisher safe. The skiff passes through the gap and returns with the fisher. This use realizes the end that organized its design and construction.
